blocks.text: **Devmaxx topic:** the reliability half of the design surface. **Goal:** survive component failure, deploy failure, region failure, and human failure.

rows: How long you can be down before it's unacceptable
How much data loss you can tolerate (measured in time)
The percentage of time the service works
The system continues operating despite failures
Switching to a backup when the primary fails
Switching back after the primary is repaired
Plan for catastrophic loss of a region/datacenter
Deliberately injecting failures to test resilience
Isolated stacks that limit blast radius

blocks.text: **RPO and RTO drive the architecture.** RPO 0 (no data loss) forces synchronous replication (which costs latency). RTO 1 hour allows manual failover; RTO 60 seconds requires automated failover with automated DNS/service-discovery updates.
**Design for the ones you can predict; build systems that make the unpredictable survivable.**
3.1 Eliminate single points of failure (SPOFs)
The SPOF checklist:

items.text: [ ] Application servers — N instances, no local state
[ ] The load balancer — two or more, or a managed one with redundancy
[ ] The database primary — replicas + automated failover
[ ] DNS — multiple nameservers; DNS itself is a SPOF you often can't control (mitigate with health-checked DNS or by not depending on DNS for critical routing)
[ ] Cache — Redis with a sentinel/cluster
[ ] Message broker — replicated
[ ] Certificate authority — use a managed cert with automated renewal
[ ] Secrets store — replicated, multi-region
[ ] The CI/CD pipeline — not on the critical path of serving traffic
[ ] The person — on-call rotation, documented runbooks

blocks.text: **"Two of everything" is the baseline.** One for you, one for the failure.
3.2 Health checks that are actually useful

items.text: **Liveness** — process health only. Restart if it fails.
**Readiness** — can this instance serve traffic right now? Remove from the LB.
**Deep health** — checks every dependency. Use it for **reporting and alerting**, not for

blocks.text: automatic restarts (you'd restart everything during a DB blip).

items.text: **Startup probe** — slow-start protection.

blocks.text: 3.3 Graceful degradation
Ask for each feature: "if this dependency is down, what still works?"

rows: Fall back to a simpler SQL search, or hide the search box
Show "processing" and retry later; queue the intent
Use a cached token list / fail-closed for sensitive ops
Fail over to a replica; if none, serve cached reads only

blocks.text: **Design the degraded state explicitly.** "It'll be fine" is not a design.
3.4 Circuit breaker

blocks.code:
CLOSED    → normal, count failures
OPEN      → fail fast (don't call the dependency), for a cooldown period
HALF_OPEN → try a few requests; success → CLOSED, failure → OPEN

blocks.text: Prevents a slow dependency from consuming all your threads. **Key detail:** the breaker should **fail fast**, not queue — queued requests are what cause fail-slow collapse.
3.5 Bulkheads
Separate resource pools per dependency (and per tenant tier) so one failure can't consume everything. Implemented as separate thread pools, connection pools, or separate instances.
3.6 Backpressure and load shedding
Propagate congestion upstream so the overload is contained:

items.text: Bounded queues; reject when full.
Return 503 with `Retry-After` rather than queueing forever.
Shed by priority: premium traffic first, batch jobs last.
**Reject work you can't do well** — a fast failure is better than a slow one that fails anyway.

blocks.text: 3.7 Chaos engineering
Deliberately inject failures in production (or a realistic staging environment):

items.text: Kill random instances.
Add latency to dependencies.
Drop packets / partition the network.
Fill disks.
Corrupt a dependency.

blocks.text: **Chaos without hypotheses is just sabotage.** The right process:

items.text: **Hypothesis**: "If region B's database fails, traffic reroutes to region A and error rate stays below X%."
**Steady state**: verify the system is healthy.
**Inject** the fault.
**Compare** against the hypothesis.
**Fix and re-run** — the fix must be automated, not manual.

blocks.text: Start in staging, then production, with a **blast-radius radius** (one instance, one AZ).
Automatic failover (Patroni / cloud-native)

blocks.code:
1. Detect: the primary fails its health check repeatedly (or loses the consensus quorum)
2. Fence: ensure the old primary can't accept writes (STONITH, or it loses its lease)
3. Elect: choose the replica with the highest applied WAL position
4. Promote: make it the primary
5. Reconfigure: update the connection endpoint (DNS/VIP/service discovery)
6. Rebuild: re-point the old primary as a replica

blocks.text: **The pitfalls:**

items.text: **Split brain** → fencing (Ch. 04 §9).
**Connection storms** → every client reconnects at once. Mitigate with pooling, backoff, and

blocks.text: staggered reconnects.

items.text: **The old primary rejoining** must be careful not to introduce divergent data. Rebuild it as a

blocks.text: replica (discard its WAL) if there's any doubt.

items.text: **Failover isn't instant.** DNS propagation can take minutes. Use health-checked DNS or a

blocks.text: dynamic endpoint (an internal service registry) to speed it up.
Manual failover
Safer (no surprise promotions) but slow (MTTR = human reaction + steps). For a 40-person company with a strong on-call, manual is often the right call. Document the runbook and practice it.
5.1 The three patterns
**Pattern A: Active-Passive (cold standby)**

items.text: Only one region serves traffic.
The standby is scaled down (or warm) and takes over on failure.
**Pros:** simple, no consistency conflicts, cost-effective.
**Cons:** failover takes minutes (scale up + DNS), RPO = the async replication lag (seconds to

blocks.text: minutes).

items.text: **Use when:** regulatory requirements or a moderate RTO.

blocks.text: **Pattern B: Active-Active (hot standby)**

blocks.code:
Region A ◀──conflict resolution──▶ Region B
      │                                  │
   both serve users in their region

items.text: Both regions serve traffic.
**Pros:** no idle cost, global latency, survives a region failure instantly.
**Cons:** data conflicts, harder engineering, costlier.
**Conflict resolution:** last-write-wins (with clock skew caveats), vector clocks, or CRDTs.
**Use when:** you have global users and latency/compliance demands.

blocks.text: **Pattern C: Multi-region with a single global writer**

blocks.code:
Region A (writer)  ◀──requests routed globally──▶  users everywhere
   Region B (hot replica, async)

items.text: Reads can be served locally from replicas; writes always go to one region.
**Pros:** no conflicts; write latency is the cost (users far from the writer pay 150 ms).
**Cons:** write latency for distant users; the writer region is a SPOF.
**Use when:** conflicts are unacceptable and your users are mostly regional.

blocks.text: 5.2 Latency numbers

blocks.code:
Same AZ:            0.5–1 ms
Same region:        2–10 ms
Cross continent:    50–150 ms

blocks.text: **Cross-region synchronous calls are poison for latency.** Design so that:

items.text: The hot path (auth check, read your data, write) is **single-region**.
Cross-region work is **asynchronous** (replication, analytics, cross-region workflows).
If you must be globally distributed, use **eventual consistency** with an explicit staleness

blocks.text: contract.
5.3 Data residency (GDPR and friends)

items.text: Data for EU users must stay in the EU (or be legally transferred).
Design: **regional shards** — route by user residency. Each region has its own primary.
Avoid a single global database that copies everything everywhere.
Implement **right-to-erasure**: delete the user's data from all replicas and backups per policy

blocks.text: (backups are usually handled by expiry + crypto-shredding).
5.4 Multi-region failover

blocks.code:
1. Detect the regional outage (health checks + external synthetic probes)
2. Decide: automatic (with a guard) or human-approved
3. Route traffic to the healthy region (DNS with a short TTL, or a global LB)
4. Fail over the write path: promote the replica in the healthy region
5. Reconcile: when the old region returns, decide how to merge (usually rebuild from the new
   primary; discard divergent writes)
6. Communicate: update status pages, support, and customers

blocks.text: **DNS TTL is the crux.** A 300-second TTL means a 5-minute failover via DNS. Use a global load balancer (Cloudflare, AWS Global Accelerator, GCP's global LB) that can shift traffic in seconds, or a very short TTL with health-checked DNS.
5.5 Split brain in multi-region
If both regions accept writes during a partition, you have two divergent timelines. Mitigations:

items.text: **Region priority**: only one region accepts writes at a time (enforced by a quorum service).
**Fencing tokens** from a global quorum (e.g. etcd in a third region, or a managed quorum).
**Conflict resolution** on merge (usually last-write-wins for idempotent operations, or

blocks.text: application-specific merging for business data).
**The only metric that matters: does the restore work, and how long does it take?**
The 3-2-1-1-0 rule

items.text: **3** copies of your data
**2** different media/technologies
**1** offsite (different region/account)
**1** offline/immutable (ransomware protection)
**0** errors (verified restores)

blocks.text: Backup types
**Point-in-time recovery (PITR)** = snapshot + continuous log archiving → restore to any moment between the snapshot and now. This is the practical gold standard for databases.
The restore drill

items.text: **Restore into a clean environment** and verify data integrity (row counts, checksums, business

blocks.text: invariants).

items.text: **Time it.** If you claim an RTO of 1 hour, you must be able to restore in 1 hour.
**Test quarterly.** A backup you haven't restored is a hypothesis, not a backup.
**Test application-level restores too** — restoring the DB isn't enough if the object storage

blocks.text: or search index is missing.
Ransomware and accidental deletion

items.text: **Object Lock / immutability** on backups (can't be deleted by a compromised credential).
**Separate credentials** for backup deletion.
**Versioned buckets** (protect against overwrite).
**Soft delete + a deletion delay.**
**Audit logs** on backup operations.
**Prefer snapshot restore over logical restore** for speed, but know logical restores catch

blocks.text: silent corruption.
Large systems divide into **cells** — self-contained stacks that each serve a slice of users.

blocks.code:
Global Traffic Router (anycast / DNS / global LB)
         ┌───────────────┬───────────────┐
         ▼               ▼               ▼
       Cell 1          Cell 2          Cell 3
    ┌────────┐      ┌────────┐      ┌────────┐
    │App     │      │App     │      │App     │
    │DB      │      │DB      │      │DB      │
    │Cache   │      │Cache   │      │Cache   │
    │Queue   │      │Queue   │      │Queue   │
    └────────┘      └────────┘      └────────┘

blocks.text: **Benefits:**

items.text: **Blast radius containment** — a bug in Cell 1 affects 1/N of users, not everyone.
**Incremental scalability** — add a cell, increase capacity by 1/N.
**Regional cells** — run cells in different regions for latency and residency.
**Testable** — a cell is a complete testable unit.

blocks.text: **Costs:**

items.text: Cross-cell queries are hard (you may need data from many cells).
Routing must be consistent (a user should stick to a cell → hash on user ID).
Global features (a user's friends in another cell) require cross-cell communication.
More infrastructure to build and operate.

blocks.text: **Used by:** Amazon (cells), Google, and many large-scale consumer systems. It's a strong fit for multi-region with data residency.
Feature flags as a reliability tool
A **kill switch** — a flag that disables a feature without a deploy — is the fastest mitigation for a bad feature. Keep kill switches for every risky feature, tested, and documented.

items.text: **Chaos experiment: kill a dependency.** Break the database in a staging environment. Verify: the circuit breaker opens, requests fail fast with 503, the connection pool doesn't exhaust, and the service recovers when the DB returns. Measure the recovery time.

**Failover drill.** Trigger an automatic database failover. Measure: detection time, promotion time, endpoint update time, and the total data loss (RPO). Then run it 5 times — the variance matters more than the best run.
**Restore drill.** Take a backup, restore it into a new environment, and time the restore. Write down the actual RTO (not the intended one).

**Chaos with a hypothesis.** Write three hypotheses about your system (e.g. "losing 2 of 5 AZs keeps the service available with <1% errors"), inject the faults, and record the results. Fix what fails and re-run.

**Multi-region design doc.** For your app, decide: active-passive or active-active? Where does the write path live? What's the RPO/RTO? How do you detect a regional outage? Write it and review it with a peer.

blocks.text: Good: "I'll run the app tier across 3 AZs with a health-checked load balancer, the database with synchronous replication to a replica in another AZ and async to a DR region. If the primary fails, Patroni promotes the most up-to-date replica. The RPO is a few seconds and the RTO is under a minute. I'll add a circuit breaker on the cache so a cache outage doesn't take down the DB."

Better: "For a global product I'll use a cell-based architecture: one cell per region, each with its own primary DB, routed by user residency. A regional outage takes out one cell and the global router shifts traffic to healthy cells. I'll use a quorum service for cross-cell coordination to prevent split brain, and I'll do quarterly restore drills with measured RTOs."
Red flags: "the cloud handles failover"; no RPO/RTO; "we'll add multi-region later"; single region with no DR plan; backups with no restore test.

selfCheck.q: **What is the difference between RPO and RTO? Give an example pair.**
selfCheck.a: **RPO** = how much data you can lose (measured in time — "5 minutes of writes"). **RTO** = how long you can be down. Example: RPO 5 min / RTO 1 hour → async replication + automated failover with DNS-based routing. RPO 0 / RTO 5 min → synchronous replication + automatic promotion + fast (non-DNS) routing.

selfCheck.q: **What RPO does synchronous replication give you, and what does it cost?**
selfCheck.a: RPO 0 (or near 0) for acknowledged writes. Cost: a network round trip per write (1–2 ms same-region, 50–150 ms cross-region), and write availability becomes coupled to the replica's health.

selfCheck.q: **List five common single points of failure in a web service.**
selfCheck.a: Single app server, single LB, the DB primary, DNS, the cache, the message broker, the secrets store, certificate renewal, and the deployment pipeline (if a deploy failure blocks fixes).

selfCheck.q: **Why shouldn't a liveness probe check the database?**
selfCheck.a: A DB blip would fail every instance's liveness check simultaneously → all instances restart at once → cold caches and connections → thundering herd → the blip becomes a full outage. Liveness should test only the process; dependency checks belong in readiness.

selfCheck.q: **What is a circuit breaker's three states and what happens in each?**
selfCheck.a: **CLOSED** = normal, failures counted. **OPEN** = fail fast immediately, don't call the dependency, for a cooldown. **HALF_OPEN** = let a few probe requests through; success closes the breaker, failure reopens it. HALF_OPEN prevents flapping.

selfCheck.q: **Why must a circuit breaker fail fast rather than queue?**
selfCheck.a: Queued requests still occupy threads, connections, and memory while waiting on a dead dependency — that's fail-slow, and it collapses the caller instead of protecting it. Failing fast frees the resources immediately and gives the caller a clear error.

selfCheck.q: **What is a bulkhead, and how is it different from a rate limiter?**
selfCheck.a: A bulkhead partitions resources (separate thread/connection pools per dependency) so one dependency can't consume them all. A rate limiter rejects excess requests to protect *capacity*; a bulkhead contains the *damage* from a failing dependency.

selfCheck.q: **Give three examples of graceful degradation.**
selfCheck.a: Cache down → serve from the DB (slower). Search down → fall back to SQL search or hide the feature. Recommendations down → hide the section. Payments down → queue the intent and show "processing".

selfCheck.q: **What's the blast-radius benefit of cell-based architecture?**
selfCheck.a: A bug or outage in one cell affects only that cell's users (1/N of the total), so the failure is contained instead of global. Cells also let you add capacity incrementally and run regions independently for latency and data residency.

selfCheck.q: **Compare active-passive and active-active multi-region.**
selfCheck.a: **Active-passive**: one region serves, the other is idle/warm; failover takes minutes (scale up + DNS); no data conflicts; cheaper; RPO = the async lag. **Active-active**: both serve; no idle cost; global latency; instant failover; but you must solve write conflicts and pay for two full regions.

selfCheck.q: **Why is synchronous cross-region replication usually rejected?**
selfCheck.a: It adds 50–150 ms to every write, which destroys write throughput and latency. Keep synchronous replication *within* a region and use async across regions with an explicit, business-approved RPO.

selfCheck.q: **What is PITR and what does it give you over a plain snapshot?**
selfCheck.a: Point-in-time recovery restores to any moment between the last snapshot and now, using continuously archived transaction logs. A snapshot alone only gets you back to the snapshot time (which could be hours of data loss). PITR typically gets you to a 0–5 minute RPO.

selfCheck.q: **What is the 3-2-1-1-0 rule?**
selfCheck.a: **3** copies of the data, on **2** different media/technologies, **1** offsite, **1** offline or immutable, and **0** errors (verified restores).

selfCheck.q: **Why is a backup you haven't restored not a backup?**
selfCheck.a: Because a backup is only useful if it can be restored correctly and in time. Files can be corrupt, the format may be wrong, the process may fail under real conditions, and the restore may exceed your RTO. An untested backup is a hypothesis.

selfCheck.q: **How do you protect backups from ransomware?**
selfCheck.a: Object Lock / immutability on the backup bucket (can't be deleted or overwritten), separate credentials for deletion, versioned buckets, MFA on destructive operations, audit logs, and keeping a copy in a separate account (so compromising one account doesn't get everything).

selfCheck.q: **What is a kill switch and when is it the fastest mitigation?**
selfCheck.a: A feature flag that instantly disables a feature without a deploy. For a new feature causing errors or excessive load, flipping the flag takes seconds, versus minutes for a rollback and hours for a new release.

selfCheck.q: **Why canary deployments reduce blast radius?**
selfCheck.a: A canary sends a small percentage (1%, then 10%) of traffic to the new version. A problem affects only that slice of users, and you detect it with canary-specific metrics before ramping. A full rollout turns a small problem into a full outage.

selfCheck.q: **What is a "connection storm" on failover, and how do you mitigate it?**
selfCheck.a: When the primary fails, every client gets an error and reconnects at once, hammering the newly promoted primary. Mitigate with connection pooling, exponential backoff with jitter, and keeping enough warm capacity on the new primary.

selfCheck.q: **What's the difference between failover and failback, and why is failback risky?**
selfCheck.a: **Failover** = switching to the backup. **Failback** = switching back to the (repaired) original. Failback is risky because the original may have divergent data or missed events while it was away — it's a common source of data loss. Mitigate by rebuilding the original as a replica before switching traffic back, and making failback a deliberate, tested operation.

selfCheck.q: **How does data residency change your architecture?**
selfCheck.a: You can no longer replicate user data across regions freely. You need regional data stores (often per-region cells or shards), residency-aware routing (a user in the EU is served by EU infrastructure), residency-aware logging/analytics, and a deletion story that covers every replica and backup.
